text: So far we've always joined two different tables. But what if the relationship you're trying to represent lives inside a single table? That's a self join — a table joined to itself.

There's no new keyword here. It's the exact same JOIN syntax you already know, just applied to one table listed twice. The classic teaching example: an employee table where each row also stores that employee's manager. Employee, aliased as e, joined to Employee again, aliased as m, on e's manager ID matching m's employee ID. Without two different aliases, SQL Server would have no way to tell the employee's row apart from the manager's row — they're both coming from the exact same table.

AdventureWorks2012 doesn't store managers quite that simply, but it has a genuinely real self-join pattern in BillOfMaterials, which records which products are components of which assembled products. Product gets joined to itself, indirectly, through BillOfMaterials — once aliased p-assembly, for the finished product, and once aliased p-component, for a part that goes into it. Same table, two roles, two aliases — exactly the self-join pattern, in real, runnable code.

A self join isn't special syntax — it's just the same table, joined to itself, with two aliases standing in for two different roles. Next lesson: chaining three or more tables together in a single query. See you there.
